lesson.title: Buffered and Precise: The Instrumentation Amplifier
lesson.summary: A three op-amp circuit that adds high-impedance input buffering and a single adjustable resistor for gain in front of a difference amplifier, making it the standard choice for pulling tiny signals off real sensors without loading them down.
lesson.body:
The plain difference amplifier has two practical limits. Its input impedance is low, since both sources drive straight into resistor networks, and its gain is locked in by four external resistors that all have to be matched precisely at once. The instrumentation amplifier fixes both problems by adding a buffered, gain-adjustable front end ahead of the difference amplifier stage already covered.

The topology uses two non-inverting op-amps, one per input line, each with a feedback resistor R back to its own inverting input, and the two inverting inputs tied together through a single shared resistor Rg. Because each input op-amp is wired as a non-inverting amplifier, it presents very high input impedance directly to the source, the same buffering behavior used in a voltage follower, so a delicate sensor sees almost no loading. The shared resistor Rg is the clever part. For a true differential signal, current flows through Rg between the two inverting inputs and gets amplified. For a common-mode signal, where both inputs rise or fall together, both op-amp outputs move together too, so no current flows through Rg at all, and that stage passes common-mode signals through with a gain of exactly 1. The two buffered, gained outputs then feed a standard difference amplifier stage, which performs the final subtraction using resistors that are easy to match precisely inside a single package.

For this three op-amp topology, the overall differential gain is G = (1 + 2R/Rg) times (Rf/Rin), where R is the matched feedback resistor on each input stage, Rg is the single shared gain-setting resistor, and Rf/Rin is the gain of the final difference-amplifier stage.

Let R = 25 kilohm on each input stage, Rg = 5 kilohm, and a unity-gain difference stage with Rf = Rin = 10 kilohm. Then 2R/Rg = (2 times 25k) divided by 5k = 10, so 1 + 2R/Rg = 11, and Rf/Rin = 10k/10k = 1. Multiplying gives G = 11 times 1 = 11. For a differential input of 10mV, the output is Vout = 11 times 10mV = 110mV, or 0.11V.

Notice that only Rg typically needs to change to adjust the overall gain, a single resistor instead of four matched ones. The buffering that lets common-mode signals pass with a gain of exactly 1 through the first stage, combined with well-matched resistors in the second stage, gives the instrumentation amplifier a much higher CMRR than a plain four-resistor difference amplifier, a distinction picked up directly in the next two concepts.
